solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Scottish bum, placed askew – he drank heavily

definitions.note: a phrase standing for a noun: one who drank heavily

indicators.note: something set askew is out of its proper line, so the preceding word is put into a new order

blocks.note: Scots word for the buttocks or a tail

explanation.surface: A Scottish tramp, his seat placed crookedly, was a heavy drinker.
explanation.walkthrough: FUDDLECAP is an old word for a drunkard; the definition is a whole clause describing the person.
explanation.definitionFit: A fuddlecap is a tippler, someone given to fuddling himself with drink, so he is one who drank heavily.

clue.text: Heads for forest under shady cover, dingy

indicators.note: heads are the leading letters of each following word

explanation.surface: Making for the woods under gloomy shade, everything dim.
explanation.definitionFit: Fusc is an old word for dark brown or dusky, so drab and dingy.

clue.text: Sheep roaming wild catches cow up in the manner of a mate

definitions.text: in the manner of a mate

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means read from bottom to top
catching something holds it inside, so one piece is enclosed

explanation.surface: A wild sheep on the loose seizes a cow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roaming wild' looks like an anagram signal; it just describes the wild sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Uxorial means relating to or befitting a wife, and a mate here is a spouse.

clue.text: Sink out of use? Pleased when it's restored

definitions.note: out of use marks the verb as obsolete

indicators.note: something restored is reworked and put back together, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A disused sink pleases its owner once restored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink out of use' pictures a disused basin; it is the verb sink, and the word is obsolete.
explanation.definitionFit: Delapse is an obsolete verb meaning to sink or slide down.

clue.text: It's familiar to refiners of silver, making it hard with generous coating

definitions.text: It's familiar to refiners of silver

indicators.note: a coating wraps right round, so the generous word surrounds the others

blocks.note: large as in liberal or generous

explanation.surface: A refinery worker would know it, hard but generously coated.
explanation.definitionFit: Litharge is lead monoxide formed when silver is refined by cupellation, so silver refiners know it well.

clue.text: For best effect it requires keeping one's hand in? Blimey, I think not

definitions.text: For best effect it requires keeping one's hand in?

explanation.surface: Advice about keeping in practice, met with a sceptical 'Blimey, I think not'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeping one's hand in' sounds like staying in practice; a horn player literally keeps a hand inside the bell.
explanation.definitionFit: The corno is the Italian name for the French horn, whose player shapes the tone with a hand in the bell.

clue.text: Misguided pleasantry about Hussite's opening idealistic social centre

indicators.note: misguided means sent the wrong way, so the letters go astray into a new order
about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go round the single one
an opening is the start, so take only the first letter

explanation.surface: A misjudged joke concerning a Hussite reformer's idealistic community.
explanation.walkthrough: Hussites were followers of Jan Hus; only the first letter matters.
explanation.definitionFit: A phalanstery was the communal building of one of Fourier's utopian socialist communities, a centre for an idealistic social scheme.

clue.text: Old master having something to get barbecue going? Not quite

indicators.note: read literally, 'not quite' tells us to remove the letters spelling the word quite from the end

blocks.note: a hardwood prized as barbecue fuel

explanation.surface: An old artist with something to start the grill, but not quite enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' normally means nearly; here it says drop QUITE from the mesquite wood.
explanation.definitionFit: MES is an obsolete form of 'master' used as a title, as in old forms of address, hence an old master.

clue.text: Aussie mutt or cat pinching last scrap from kitchen

indicators.note: the last scrap is the final bit, so only the end letter is used
pinching means grabbing and holding, so the cat encloses the letter

blocks.note: British informal word for a cat

explanation.surface: A dog or cat stealing leftovers from the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: A mog or moggy is everyday British slang for a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang a mong is a mongrel dog, a mutt of mixed breed.

clue.text: Business from abroad and so new

definitions.note: from abroad marks a foreign word

explanation.surface: Trade coming from overseas is therefore fresh.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergon is Greek for work, so it is a foreign word for one's business or task.

clue.text: Marine creature, live when caught by tail (8, two words)

indicators.note: something caught by another is held within it, so these pieces go inside

explanation.surface: A sea creature that stays alive when grabbed by its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: Tail here is the bottom one sits on.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea beast is any large creature of the ocean, a marine creature.

clue.text: Nasty sores I twice got following menu? Result of eating bad food

indicators.note: something nasty is in a bad way, so the letters are messed up
following means coming after, so the shuffled part goes behind the menu

blocks.note: a menu is a list of dishes

explanation.surface: After a restaurant meal someone came out in nasty sores, food poisoning the likely cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Listeriosis is an illness caused by listeria bacteria, typically caught from contaminated food.

clue.text: Is Frodo's last burden what shows constancy in volume?

indicators.note: last points at the final letter of the name before it

blocks.note: end letter of the hobbit's name

explanation.surface: A Tolkien-ish question about whether Frodo's final load shows a steady volume.
explanation.definitionFit: An isochore is a line on a graph joining points of equal volume, so it displays volume held constant.

clue.text: Very drunk, ultimately blotto as usual

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the next word counts

explanation.surface: Someone is very drunk, completely blotto in the end, as is their habit.
explanation.definitionFit: SOLITO is a musical direction meaning play in the usual or customary manner.

clue.text: Flimsy beachwear, one has seaweed stuck to one

indicators.note: one thing stuck to another sits right beside it, so the two pieces join end to end

blocks.note: tang is a kind of coarse seaweed
A as the indefinite article meaning one

explanation.surface: A skimpy swimsuit with some seaweed clinging to it after a dip.
explanation.definitionFit: A tanga is a very brief bikini-style swimming costume or briefs, about as flimsy as beachwear gets.

clue.text: Like waves on the rocks, or a bore

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective in the phrase 'a crashing bore'

blocks.note: first meaning: breaking noisily against something
second meaning: the intensifier that idiomatically goes with bore, meaning utter

explanation.walkthrough: The second half works through the set phrase: a tedious person is called a crashing bore.
explanation.definitionFit: Waves smashing on rocks are crashing, and the same word is the stock intensifier for an utterly tedious person.

clue.text: Old philosopher, form of Stoic absorbing what's current in Cambridge

indicators.note: a form of a word here is a reshaped version of its letters
absorbing means taking in, so the rearranged letters surround the other piece

explanation.surface: An ancient thinker of the Stoic school, taking in the latest ideas at Cambridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like up-to-date; it means a flowing river, the Cam.
explanation.definitionFit: An Occamist was a medieval follower of William of Occam, the nominalist philosopher of Occam's razor.

clue.text: Salad ingredient, great with eggs around

indicators.note: around says the eggs wrap about the other word, enclosing it

blocks.note: main as in chief or great

explanation.surface: A salad component is wonderful served with eggs around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Romaine is cos lettuce, a standard leafy salad ingredient.

clue.text: Way of working is undoing for police force abroad

blocks.note: unties = is undoing, as with a knot

explanation.surface: A bad working method is the downfall of a foreign police force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undoing' looks like ruin; it is the plain verb, unfastening.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mounties are the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a police force outside Britain.

clue.text: Where soldiers were billeted in event alongside the fleet?

indicators.note: alongside places one item directly next to the other, so they join in sequence

explanation.surface: A question about where troops lodged when the navy was in port.
explanation.definitionFit: A casern is a barracks, a building where soldiers were lodged in garrison towns in former times.

clue.text: Hot stuff disowned by band, not pro

indicators.note: to be disowned is to be cast off, so the following word is dropped from the longer one

blocks.note: hot means stolen or illicit, so hot stuff is smuggled goods

explanation.surface: Spicy music rejected by a group of players who are against it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot stuff' suggests chillies or passion; here hot is slang for illicit goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Contra is Latin for against, the opposite of pro in the pairing pros and cons.

clue.text: Principals in theatre hit overwhelmed by claps?

definitions.note: the claps are of thunder; the answer is the mass noun

indicators.note: principals are the leading players, so take the leading letters

blocks.note: first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Stars of a theatrical success swamped by applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Claps' suggests applause; the definition is claps of thunder.
explanation.definitionFit: Thunder comes in claps, the sudden crashing sound following lightning.

clue.text: Copy page in antique, its first

indicators.note: in places the page letter inside the other piece

explanation.surface: A copied page in an old book, the first one in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Its' refers back to antique, whose first letter is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A replica is a copy or reproduction of an original.

clue.text: Those from the ministry putting work unit into nick once

indicators.note: putting something into another places it inside, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: old thieves' slang verb meaning to steal

explanation.surface: Government officials putting a work unit into an old prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick looks like a prison; it is the old slang verb to steal, CLY.
explanation.definitionFit: The clergy are the ordained ministers of the church, people who have gone into the ministry.

clue.text: Male interrupting girl playfully is offensive

indicators.note: interrupting means breaking into the middle, so the male piece goes inside

blocks.note: a playful, affectionate term for a girl

explanation.surface: A man butting in on a girl in fun is being objectionable.
explanation.walkthrough: Offensive is meant in its military sense: to push is to mount an attack.
explanation.definitionFit: An army that pushes is making a forward attack, so it is on the offensive.

clue.text: Aegises deployed in historic blockade

indicators.note: troops deployed are spread into new positions, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Shields brought into play during a famous siege.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Historic' marks the definition as an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: To assiege is an archaic form of besiege, to surround a place and cut it off as in a blockade.

clue.text: Foreign gentleman framed by Veronese, mounted

indicators.note: something framed by a word lies within its edges
in a down entry, mounted means going upward, so read bottom to top

explanation.surface: A portrait of a foreign nobleman framed and hung by the Italian painter Veronese.
explanation.definitionFit: Señor is the Spanish title for a man, the equivalent of Mr or sir.

clue.text: Wild flower, green and pale

explanation.surface: A wildflower with greenish-pale colouring.
explanation.definitionFit: Gowan is the Scots name for the daisy, a common wild flower.

clue.text: A bit like Jaques's schoolboy, beginning to lick inside cone

indicators.note: the beginning is the opening letter only
inside puts the letter within the other piece

blocks.note: a small volcanic cone, as in the Auvergne

explanation.surface: A schoolboy from Shakespeare getting the start of a lick inside an ice-cream cone.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques's seven-ages speech in As You Like It has 'the whining schoolboy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Puly means whining or puling, somewhat like Shakespeare's whining schoolboy.

clue.text: Milksop receives X in liquescent manner

indicators.note: receiving something means taking it in, so the second piece goes inside the first

blocks.note: a molly is an effeminate, feeble man

explanation.surface: A weakling is handed a kiss, and melts.
explanation.walkthrough: X looks like a kiss or a mark; it is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquescent means melting or turning liquid, so acting moltenly is behaving in a melted, fluid way.

clue.text: Cry of pain let loose by nithing?

definitions.text: Cry of pain let loose by nithing?

blocks.clueFragment: Cry of pain let loose by nithing?
blocks.note: surface reading: an obscure-looking word suggests a strange creature crying out
setter's reading: a nithing is a coward, the sort to shout loudly when hurt

explanation.surface: A shriek of pain released by some cowardly wretch.
explanation.walkthrough: Nithing is an old word for a coward or villain, who would loudly cry out when hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: A yell is a loud cry, often of pain or fear.

clue.text: Like brands discontinued as part of main US trade

definitions.note: discontinued marks the word as obsolete

indicators.note: as part of says the letters sit within the run of words that follow

explanation.surface: Product brands withdrawn as part of the main American trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontinued' sounds like dropped products but signals that the answer is an obsolete word.
explanation.definitionFit: Inust is an old word meaning burnt in, which is how brands are marked on cattle.

clue.text: Wife on reflection to long for 2, 3 or 4?

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so the word is read the other way

blocks.note: a rib is a wife, from Eve made of Adam's rib

explanation.surface: A wife, thinking it over, longs for two, three or four of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers are golf scores: one under par on a par 3, 4 or 5 hole.
explanation.definitionFit: A birdie is a golf score one stroke under par, so 2 on a par-three, 3 on a par-four, 4 on a par-five.

clue.text: Little old coin, Sun King's No. 2 on face

indicators.note: number two picks out the second letter of the word it belongs to

explanation.surface: A small antique coin with Louis XIV's second-in-command on its face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun King' is Louis XIV, but here Sun and King are split.
explanation.definitionFit: A solidare was an old coin of small value, mentioned by Shakespeare.

clue.text: Party member sparing nothing in effort

indicators.note: sparing means leaving out, and nothing is the zero-shaped letter left out

explanation.surface: A political activist who holds nothing back in their exertions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sparing nothing' looks like all-out effort; it means losing O, nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A try is an attempt, an effort at something, as in giving it a go.

clue.text: Silt swirling with rains near on our roads?

definitions.note: an adjective for the left side

indicators.note: swirling stirs things round, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Mud swirled about by downpours on the roads near us.
explanation.walkthrough: On British roads, which drive on the left, the near side of a car is its left side.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinistral means left-hand, and in Britain the nearside of a vehicle is the left, the kerb side.
